column1: L0 holds everything that must survive a tick and nothing else.
L0 is the only backwards path in the system, is always read at a lag of at least one tick, and is the component whose existence makes the within-tick dependency graph acyclic.
L0's input is StateUpdate committed once at the end of a tick, plus the ValueFunctionArtefact from the slow loop.
L0's output is StateSnapshot, taken once at the top of a tick and read by L1, L2, L3 and L5.
L0 is stateful by definition and the only mutable component, with mutation confined to a single commit point per tick.

Three dependencies break the intended one-directional pipeline: λ_SOC is a dual of the Planner's own problem, peak_to_go and the §19(2) qualification state depend on realised history, and the commitment ledger is Execution output feeding a later Planner run.
The within-tick graph is a DAG: every arrow points right and the single backwards edge is not traversed until the tick has ended.
The within-tick DAG is what makes each seam independently recordable, replayable and property-testable, and is the foundation of the compliance architecture.
The DAG is mechanically verifiable: T3 instruments every read and write during a replay and asserts no read of a same-tick write.
L0 holds V(SOC, peakState, qualState) as a concave PWL curve, and the Planner obtains λ_SOC as its subgradient at the optimum and reports it for diagnostics.

A global mutable service, a fixed-point iteration within a tick, and Valuation calling the Planner each produce a system where two components can legitimately read different answers to the same question during the same tick, at which point nothing is reproducible and no seam test means anything.
L0 holds six items, and its field tables mirror C5 exactly, introducing no field C5 does not carry.
Peak state is carried per regime and not per site, because a site under AtypicalHlzf and a volumetric charge has two peak accumulators over different slot sets and different period bounds.
The qualification margin, not just the status, is what the value function conditions on, because a binary flag tells the engine nothing until it is too late.
Confirmed ledger entries are hard constraints and Pending entries are probabilistic exposure that the Planner models as a scenario-dependent position.
The Pending/Confirmed distinction is what lets the continuous intraday loop re-optimise without either double-selling or ignoring live exposure.
The value function is the one L0 section that does not arrive through C5.
A ValueFunctionArtefact carries specHash, fittedAt, validityHorizon, method, conditioning, curves and diagnostics.
The value function method is one of RollingHorizonDE, Sddp or BackwardRecursion.
The value function conditioning is over peakBuckets, qualStates and calendarBuckets.
Breakpoints are pairs (e_i, v_i) for i = 0..n with strictly decreasing slopes.
L0 stores the value function artefact's identity and the loaded curves, not a model object.
The value curve is a table of breakpoints and evaluating it is a PWL lookup.
L0 also carries vSocStale, stateDriftSignal and refreshRequested from C5 §8, consumed by the slow loop trigger logic.
L0 holds the manifest identities of every artefact the run is entitled to read: scenario generator, reduced ensemble, fill model, activation model, value function, market calendar and tzdata.
L0 holds artefact identities only, and the bytes live in the Belief cold tier addressed by hash.
L0 holds no beliefs: forecasts, prices, ensembles and quality values live in L1, and L0 holds only the summary quality state that must survive a tick.
L0 holds no plans: PlanResult is recorded for diagnostics and settlement but is not state, and the only Planner output that survives a tick is a ledger entry.
L0 holds no artefact contents, only identities.
L0 holds no wall-clock time.
L0 holds no derived caches: anything recomputable is recomputed, so that a restored snapshot is unambiguously equal to the one persisted.
There is exactly one writer of L0 — the tick driver's Commit — and the StateUpdate it commits is assembled from two sources.
L5 owns the settled and confirmed sections: fills, awards, activations, meter reality, P&L attribution and error decomposition.
The driver reconciles submitted intent against Execution's dispositions to produce the Pending and OpenOrder delta.
Because C4 carries no Planner reasoning, L5 cannot see a still-live order, but the driver can because it holds both payloads.
The two-contributor, one-payload, one-atomic-commit arrangement preserves C4 §8 and ADR-006 simultaneously and keeps one-backwards-edge literally true.
The tick is: snapshot L0, snapshot L1, evaluate L2, solve L3, execute L4, settle L5 combined with the driver ledger delta, then commit to L0 against the expected generation.
Snapshot and Commit are the only interactions with L0, and everything between them operates on the snapshot value.
L0.Snapshot() is the only read API: there is no L0.Get(field), no property accessor and no injected store reference.
A component holds a StateSnapshot value and does not hold L0.
StateSnapshot is an immutable record and nothing in it aliases a live structure.
The ledger is copied into the snapshot, at a cost of O(open orders + awarded blocks), which is tens of entries.
The value function is referenced by hash into an immutable, content-addressed curve cache which cannot change under the reader.
StateSnapshot carries a contentHash and appears in the inputHashes of every payload produced during the tick, which puts the state version into the Merkle chain.
StateSnapshot carries generation and asOfGeneration so a consumer can state the lag it is working with, which is what makes the lag priceable rather than hidden.
The snapshot-only read API is the same structural move as ADR-004's missing asOf overload: to read a same-tick write a developer would have to add a getter to L0, a visible change to that component.
There is one commit per tick, and Commit takes the expected generation and fails if it does not match.
A generation mismatch on Commit means two ticks overlapped, which is a driver defect and goes to HALT.
Commit is atomic: the update is applied to all sections or to none, and no partially-updated intermediate state is visible to any reader.
Commit is validating: C5's invariants plus C0's universal set are checked on receipt, and consumer-side validation failure is a HALT.
No-same-tick-read is enforced by three mechanisms of increasing strength: the type system, a reflection test, and the T3 acyclicity audit.
The type system catches the accidental case at compile time at no cost, because StateSnapshot is a value with no back-reference and L0 exposes no getter.
A reflection test over L0's public surface asserts no read method other than Snapshot(), catching someone adding a convenience accessor later.

The T3 acyclicity audit instruments every read and write during a replay as (tickId, component, section, direction) and asserts no read of a section written in the same tickId, catching the deliberate or indirect case including via a shared helper.
The audit's own overhead must not change results, so the audit day is run with and without instrumentation and artefact hashes are compared.

A fourth independent check falls out of the Merkle chain for free: every payload's inputHashes must contain the tick's StateSnapshot.contentHash, so a same-tick read would have to reference a generation hash that did not exist when the payload was sealed.
L0 is the entire engine state, because everything else is either pure, a read over immutable data, or external.
An engine restart loads a StateSnapshot and continues.
L0 persistence is content-addressed with an append-only journal supplying order.
A journal record carries tickId, generation, parentSnapshotHash, updateHash, snapshotHash, six section hashes and a record checksum.
L0 sections are hashed and stored independently, and a snapshot is the ordered list of its section hashes.
Peak state and the value function change rarely while the ledger and the quality summary churn every tick.
Structural sharing means a typical commit writes one or two small blobs and one journal record rather than a full state image.
Restart hydrates L0 by fetching sections by hash.

Restart scans the journal backwards to the last record with a valid checksum, verifies every referenced section blob resolves and rehashes correctly, hydrates the snapshot at generation g, reconciles against Execution, and resumes at tickId + 1.
Any section blob mismatch on restart is a HALT for an unreadable state store.
On restart L1's cursor is repositioned from asOf and the hot window refilled from warm and cold, and nothing else needs restoring because L2, L3 and L5 are pure.
A restored snapshot is field-identical to the one persisted and its recomputed content hash matches.
The journal record is the commit point and is written after the section blobs are durable.
A crash during steps 1 to 6 of the tick leaves generation g unchanged and the tick replays.
A crash after section blobs but before the journal record leaves generation g plus orphan blobs, which are unreferenced garbage collected by hash sweep, and the tick replays.
A crash during the journal append leaves a torn tail, which is truncated at the last valid checksum, and the tick replays.
A crash after the journal record leaves generation g+1 committed and the engine resumes at tickId + 1.
Blobs are written to a temporary name, fsynced, then renamed, and the journal is appended with a per-record checksum and fsynced.
A tick that does not reach Commit leaves L0 byte-identical at the previous generation.

Because a replayed tick begins from the identical StateSnapshot and identical recorded belief inputs, and because L2, L3 and L5 are pure and the solver deterministic, the replayed tick produces byte-identical outputs to the one that was lost.
L0 is the entire engine state but not the entire world state, and the venue is the authority on what was submitted.
A crash between order submission and commit leaves orders live at Execution that the restored ledger does not know about, and replaying the tick blindly would re-submit them.

Restart performs a reconciliation pass before the first tick: query Execution for live and recently-terminal orders and awards, diff against the restored ledger, insert every unmatched acknowledged order or award via a synthetic StateUpdate tagged Reconciliation, and commit it as generation g+1 so the replayed tick becomes g+2.
The reconciliation update is a first-class, recorded artefact and not a repair script.
Because reconciliation is a recorded artefact, the every-award-has-a-ledger-entry invariant is checkable across a restart boundary rather than vacuously true because the award was forgotten.

The slow loop is not a layer and is not in the tick path: it runs on C_slow, reads L0 plus cold-tier artefacts, and writes exactly one thing, a versioned ValueFunctionArtefact whose identity is committed to L0.
The slow loop never blocks a tick.
If the slow loop has not run, the Planner uses the last valid V with a staleness penalty.
The periodic slow-loop trigger fires daily at a configured local time, after the day's ensemble artefact is published, and is a staleness trigger.
The validity-expiry trigger fires when asOf minus fittedAt exceeds validityHorizon and is a staleness trigger.
The state-drift trigger fires when stateDriftSignal is above a configured threshold and is a staleness trigger.
The explicit-request trigger fires when Settlement sets refreshRequested and is a staleness trigger.
The accounting-rollover trigger fires when periodEnd is crossed and realisedPeak resets, and is an invalidation trigger.
The qualification-transition trigger fires on a qualificationStatus change or when qualCritical is set, and is an invalidation trigger.
The regime-change trigger fires when a regime becomes active or inactive, and is an invalidation trigger.
The staleness versus invalidation distinction is load-bearing and is easy to collapse by accident.
A stale curve is an out-of-date approximation of the right curve: it attracts stalenessPenalty shrinkage of its slopes and the engine carries on.
An invalidated curve is the wrong curve: one fitted under Qualified says nothing useful about an AtRisk world, and one fitted against last month's realisedPeak prices a floor that no longer exists.
Invalidation forces DEFENSIVE until a refit lands, because shrinking the slopes of a curve conditioned on the wrong state does not make it less wrong.
The slow-loop horizon must be long enough to see the end of the accounting period, otherwise the truncation the value function exists to price is present inside the value function itself.
H_slow is at least the maximum over active regimes of (periodEnd − t) plus a tail margin.
For AnnualLeistungspreis and IntensiveUse the slow-loop horizon is up to a year of quarter-hours, about 35,000 slots.
The annual horizon is why the slow loop cannot simply run the Planner's formulation at a longer horizon and why it needs a state-space method of its own.
The slow loop uses coarsened time: 15-minute resolution in the near field and hourly or 4-hourly in the far field, with the coarsening schedule part of the FeatureSpecHash.

The slow loop uses a longer-horizon, lower-resolution ensemble generated by the same joint model as the tick-loop ensemble, so the dependence structure is consistent between what V was fitted against and what the Planner optimises against.
Assembling the slow-loop ensemble from marginals would reintroduce exactly the bias ADR-005 exists to prevent, at the horizon where it matters most.
V is fitted conditional on the discrete state and is concave in SOC given that state.
Concavity is enforced by projecting the fit onto the concave hull and validated at the contract boundary by strictly decreasing slopes.
Because V is concave and enters as a maximisation term, the PWL needs no binaries and the LP relaxation is exact, which is the property that makes it affordable in the tick.
Genuine non-concavity from the §19(2) qualification cliff is represented as a separate discrete dimension of the conditioning with a concave curve inside each cell, not smoothed away.
If a fit is non-concave and the projection loses material value, that is a signal that a conditioning dimension is missing rather than that the projection needs loosening.
Every reachable cell of the conditioning table must have a curve or a declared fallback cell.
An unreachable-in-training but reachable-in-operation cell is exactly where the engine will be when something unusual happens.
There is no settled answer on the value function method, and pretending otherwise would be the wrong kind of confidence.

The rolling-horizon deterministic equivalent solves the multi-stage problem over the reduced ensemble as one deterministic-equivalent LP or MILP, parametrically in initial SOC, with V(e) the optimal value as a function of that SOC.

The rolling-horizon deterministic equivalent reuses the Planner's own formulation and backend so there is no second physics model to keep in sync, is concave by construction in the LP case, and is the fastest route to something trustworthy.

The rolling-horizon deterministic equivalent has perfect foresight within a scenario, ignoring non-anticipativity beyond whatever stage structure is imposed, so it is systematically optimistic rather than merely noisy.
The rolling-horizon deterministic equivalent's size grows as S × H_slow, which bites hardest at exactly the annual horizon that matters.
SDDP-style approximate dynamic programming samples scenario paths on forward passes and adds supporting hyperplanes to a concave outer approximation of the value-to-go on backward passes.

SDDP handles multi-stage non-anticipativity correctly, its cut set is itself a concave PWL so no separate fitting or hull projection is needed, it scales in horizon rather than scenario count, and it provides a convergence bound so whether V is converged is answerable.
SDDP requires stagewise independence, which price processes violate, so it needs an explicit Markov lattice over a low-dimensional exogenous state, and that lattice is itself a modelling decision.
The discrete qualification state multiplies SDDP's problem count, and SDDP has the highest implementation and tuning cost of the three methods.
Backward recursion discretises (SOC, peakState, qualState) and recurses backwards over the coarsened slot grid taking weighted expectations over the ensemble at each step.

Backward recursion is conceptually simple and exactly correct on its own discretisation, handles the discrete cliff and any non-concavity natively, and produces the entire conditioning table in one sweep.
Backward recursion suffers the curse of dimensionality, and because peakState is a running max it is a path variable that must be discretised too.
Coarse peak buckets misprice precisely the threshold region that dominates the BTM business case.
Backward recursion is tractable only with aggressive coarsening and its coarsening error is hard to bound.

The recommended sequencing is to start with the rolling-horizon deterministic equivalent, run backward recursion on a coarse grid as an independent cross-check that the cliff is priced at all, and treat SDDP as the target once the state space and conditioning dimensions have stopped moving.
Disagreement between the deterministic equivalent and backward recursion around the qualification threshold is the signal that matters.
Whatever method is running, the deterministic-equivalent version remains as a reference oracle for small instances.

Method choice, grid resolution and scenario count are recorded in diagnostics and in the FeatureSpecHash, so a change of method is a change of artefact and shows up in the Merkle chain rather than as an unexplained shift in behaviour.
A better V improves every downstream decision — every tick, every gate, every market — because it is the only thing pricing everything beyond H_plan.
A better V costs nothing additional in the tick loop, because the Planner's expense is a function of the number of breakpoints and not of how well those breakpoints were fitted.
A curve fitted by a month of SDDP work and a curve fitted by a crude heuristic cost the solver the same.

The asymmetry of unbounded upside in fit quality against zero marginal runtime cost is rare, and it is why the slow loop deserves disproportionate research attention relative to its share of the codebase.
The measurement of V's quality is whether a better V produces better realised P&L, evaluated through C5's attribution rather than through the fit's own objective.
realisedPeak is a max over the settled prefix only.
The unsettled gap exists because meter data is published with a lag — provisional telemetry in minutes to hours, final metered values in days — and market settlement is later still.
peakIsProvisional and unsettledGapFrom are the two fields that make the unsettled gap visible rather than implicit.
The Planner uses its own modelled POI trajectory over the gap as a provisional peak contribution.
The epigraph floor is zPeak ≥ max(realisedPeak, max over τ in [unsettledGapFrom, t) of p̂_poi[τ]).
p̂_poi is the engine's own trajectory over the gap, telemetered where telemetry exists and modelled from the plan and the load and PV beliefs where it does not.
The gap is the most recent window, so it is disproportionately likely to contain a peak the engine just caused.
Where the gap trajectory is itself uncertain it receives the same CVaR treatment as the forward peak and picks up riskProfile.peakSafetyMarginKw.
The gap asymmetry is deliberate: overstating the provisional peak costs a little optimisation freedom while understating it can cost an entire period's demand charge.
realisedPeak, the settled quantity, is required to be non-decreasing within a period.

The Planner's provisional working peak is a different quantity from realisedPeak and may legitimately exceed the peak that eventually settles, because the modelled gap contribution is deliberately biased high.
provisionalPeak is always at least realisedPeak, and provisionalPeak is not required to be at most the eventual settled peak.
When settlement arrives, unsettledGapFrom advances, realisedPeak may step up, and the modelled gap contribution is discarded rather than blended.
The peak step on settlement arrival is a stateDriftSignal contribution, which is the correct response because the fitted V was conditioned on the old peak state.
unsettledGapFrom is non-decreasing and never exceeds the current slot.
Gap length is a first-class quality signal, and a gap that stops advancing means the meter feed is dead.
Beyond a configured maxGapSlots the peak floor is almost entirely modelled rather than measured, which escalates the degradation mode.
Peak protection cannot be protected against a quantity nobody is measuring.
isFinal and peakIsProvisional are not the same axis.
A provisional peak comes from telemetry and preliminary meter reads and becomes final when the settled meter series arrives for those slots.
A provisional imbalance comes from the preliminary imbalance price and becomes final at reBAP final publication, often weeks later.
A provisional award is acknowledged but unsettled and becomes final at the market settlement statement.
The provisional/final flag is carried into every downstream artefact so that a P&L number can always be qualified.
A restatement is a StateUpdate with revisionOf set, and L0 does not overwrite.

The L0 journal is append-only exactly as the Belief cold tier is: the current state is the fold of the journal, and a restatement appends a new entry carrying the corrected sections at a new generation.
A restatement takes effect at the generation where it arrived, not retroactively, so a replay from a manifest sees the restatement exactly when the engine saw it.
Append-only journalling is the L0 analogue of ADR-004's bitemporality and is the reason the journal is append-only rather than a mutable row per field.
A restatement is a distinct cause from a forecast error and must not be absorbed into the forecastError bucket.
A restatement that lands after an accounting period has closed is booked to the period it belongs to and flagged, never smeared into the current one.
A restatement never triggers a re-plan of past ticks; it contributes to stateDriftSignal and, if material, triggers a slow-loop refit.
Past decisions were correct given what was known, and that does not stop being true because the data improved.
State machine tests enumerate the permitted transitions of each discrete state and assert the forbidden ones throw rather than being absorbed.
qualificationStatus is directional within a qualification year: Qualified to AtRisk to Lost is reachable and Lost to Qualified inside the same year is not.
peakIsProvisional is a one-way latch per slot range: provisional to final, never back.
The permitted ledger status transitions are Pending to Confirmed to Settled, and Pending to Cancelled, and nothing else.

Restart-mid-tick replay determinism is tested by fault-injecting a process kill at each of the seven lifecycle steps, restarting, replaying, and asserting the resulting generation-g+1 snapshot hash equals the crash-free run's.
The kill between blob write and journal append is a named fixture asserting orphan blobs are collected and the tick replays cleanly.
The kill after L4 submission but before commit is a named fixture asserting the reconciliation pass reconstructs the ledger exactly and the replayed tick does not double-submit.

Commit protocol tests assert that Commit with a stale expected generation fails, that two overlapping ticks cannot both commit, that a partially-applied update is not observable, and that a reflection test finds no read method other than Snapshot().
The acyclicity audit meta-test asserts that enabling the read/write recorder does not change any artefact hash.
The realisedPeak reset slot must equal CivilCalendar.LocalMidnight(periodStart) expressed as a SlotId, not UTC midnight and not a fixed offset from the previous reset.
Both Europe/Berlin DST transition days are fixtures for the L0 tests.
The March and October month boundaries reset at local midnight despite the UTC offset change.
The accounting period containing the spring-forward day is 92 slots shorter than a naive 96-times-days computation and the period containing the autumn day 100 slots longer.
The annual accounting boundary behaves identically to the monthly one under DST.
For AtypicalHlzf the HLZF slot subset is recomputed from the calendar table for the new period rather than being carried across.
A settlement arrival that raises realisedPeak above the previously modelled gap contribution is handled without an assertion failure.
A stalled unsettled gap beyond maxGapSlots escalates the mode.

Value function tests assert concavity of every curve, conditioning coverage of every reachable cell, that staleness produces vSocStale and the stalenessPenalty path rather than a failure, that invalidation forces DEFENSIVE and not merely a penalty, and that a refit arriving mid-run changes the artefact identity in L0 and appears in the Merkle chain.
Durability tests assert that a torn blob write, a torn journal tail, and a section-hash mismatch on load each produce the declared outcome, with HALT for the last.
A snapshot restored from shared sections is field-identical to the in-memory original.
Round-tripping a full year of journal reproduces the final snapshot hash.
No component reads an L0 section written during the same tickId, and violation is a HALT audited by T3.
There is exactly one Commit per tickId, succeeding only against the expected generation, and violation is a HALT.
Every payload produced within a tick carries that tick's StateSnapshot.contentHash in inputHashes, and violation is a HALT.
The L0 journal is append-only and current state is the fold of the journal, never an in-place edit, and violation is a HALT.
The Planner's provisional peak floor is at least realisedPeak and is not required to be at most the eventual settled peak, and violation of the lower side is a HALT.
A change to V's discrete conditioning state invalidates V, forcing mode at least DEFENSIVE until refit, rather than marking it stale, and violation escalates.
